claim: Excitatory synaptic inputs to hippocampal inhibitory interneurons can undergo Hebbian, associative, or non-associative plasticity in vitro.
source: In vitro work revealed that excitatory synaptic inputs to hippocampal inhibitory interneurons could undergo Hebbian, associative, or non-associative plasticity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior in vitro work.

claim: Behavioral and learning-dependent reorganization of pyramidal cell-interneuron connections has been demonstrated by measuring spike transmission probabilities in pyramidal cell-interneuron spike cross-correlations.
source: Both behavioral and learning-dependent reorganization of these connections has also been demonstrated by measuring spike transmission probabilities in pyramidal cell-interneuron spike cross-correlations that indicate monosynaptic connections.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Light application and associated firing alteration of pyramidal and interneuron populations led to lasting changes in pyramidal-interneuron connection weights.
source: Light application and associated firing alteration of pyramidal and interneuron populations led to lasting changes in pyramidal-interneuron connection weights as indicated by spike transmission changes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Spike transmission alterations were predicted by the light-mediated changes in the number of pre- and postsynaptic spike pairing events.
source: Spike transmission alterations were predicted by the light-mediated changes in the number of pre- and postsynaptic spike pairing events and by firing rate changes of interneurons but not pyramidal cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Spike transmission alterations were predicted by firing rate changes of interneurons but not pyramidal cells.
source: Spike transmission alterations were predicted by the light-mediated changes in the number of pre- and postsynaptic spike pairing events and by firing rate changes of interneurons but not pyramidal cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Activity-dependent associative and non-associative reorganization of pyramidal-interneuron connections can be triggered by optogenetic modification of firing rate and spike synchrony.
source: This work demonstrates the presence of activity-dependent associative and non-associative reorganization of pyramidal-interneuron connections triggered by the optogenetic modification of the firing rate and spike synchrony of cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Plastic reorganization of brain circuits needed for learning and other cognitive functions involves not only principal cells but also local inhibitory interneurons.
source: It is increasingly recognized that plastic reorganization of brain circuits needed for learning and other cognitive functions involves not only principal cells but also local inhibitory interneurons (Buzsáki, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Excitatory connections onto inhibitory interneurons are often plastic.
source: A large body of work has demonstrated that excitatory connections onto inhibitory interneurons, as well as inhibitory connections on principal cells, are often plastic (Kullmann and Lamsa, 2007; McBain and Kauer, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Inhibitory connections on principal cells are often plastic.
source: A large body of work has demonstrated that excitatory connections onto inhibitory interneurons, as well as inhibitory connections on principal cells, are often plastic (Kullmann and Lamsa, 2007; McBain and Kauer, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The rules governing the plasticity of excitatory synapses on inhibitory interneurons are not always similar to that targeting other principal cells.
source: However, the rules governing the plasticity of excitatory synapses on inhibitory interneurons are not always similar to that targeting other principal cells (Bartos et al., 2011; Lamsa et al., 2007; Pelkey et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the CA1 region of the hippocampus, plasticity rules can be different depending on the experimental conditions and fibers stimulated.
source: Even in the CA1 region of the hippocampus, plasticity rules can be different, depending on the experimental conditions and fibers stimulated.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Some pyramidal-interneuron cell connections show anti-Hebbian non-associative plasticity.
source: Although in the majority of cases some pyramidal-interneuron cell connections show anti-Hebbian non-associative plasticity, others show weight changes that are governed by Hebbian rules (Le Roux et al., 2013; Nissen et al., 2010; Topolnik et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Some pyramidal-interneuron cell connections show weight changes that are governed by Hebbian rules.
source: Although in the majority of cases some pyramidal-interneuron cell connections show anti-Hebbian non-associative plasticity, others show weight changes that are governed by Hebbian rules (Le Roux et al., 2013; Nissen et al., 2010; Topolnik et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: CCK cells in the hippocampus do not seem to possess plastic synapses with their excitatory inputs.
source: In addition, some inhibitory interneuron types in the hippocampus do not seem to possess plastic synapses with their excitatory inputs, such as the CCK cells (Nissen et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Plastic alterations can occur between afferent excitatory fibers and CA1 interneurons in vivo during anesthesia.
source: In vivo work, primarily during anesthesia, has also demonstrated that plastic alterations can occur between afferent excitatory fibers and CA1 interneurons (Buzsáki and Eidelberg, 1982; Lau et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Stimulation of afferent excitatory fibers can either up- or downregulate evoked spike responses in CA1 interneurons, depending on the interneuron subtype.
source: This work showed that stimulation of these fibers could either up- or downregulate evoked spike responses, depending on the interneuron subtype.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Knowledge about the precise reorganization of pyramidal-interneuron connections during behavior is limited because of the technical challenge of directly performing patch-clamp recordings from monosynaptically connected pyramidal cell-interneuron pairs during such conditions.
source: However, our knowledge about the precise reorganization of pyramidal-interneuron connections during behavior is limited because of the technical challenge of directly performing patch-clamp recordings from monosynaptically connected pyramidal cell-interneuron pairs during such conditions.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the technical limitations of the field.

claim: It is possible to study pyramidal-interneuron connections indirectly by identifying monosynaptically connected pyramidal cell-interneuron pairs using cross-correlation analysis of spike timing and measuring spike transmission probability between them.
source: It is, however, possible to study these connections indirectly by identifying monosynaptically connected pyramidal cell-interneuron pairs by using cross-correlation analysis of the spike timing and measuring spike transmission probability between them (Csicsvari et al., 1998; Csicsvari et al., 2003; Marshall et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Early work demonstrated the behavioral state-dependent modulation of pyramidal-interneuron connections.
source: Early work demonstrated the behavioral state-dependent modulation of such connections (Csicsvari et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Changes in spike transmission probability have been seen in the prefrontal cortex during behavioral tasks.
source: Moreover, changes in spike transmission probability have been seen in the prefrontal cortex during behavioral tasks (Fujisawa et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Spatial learning can cause lasting changes in pyramidal-interneuron connections in the hippocampus.
source: In the hippocampus, spatial learning can cause lasting changes in these connections (Dupret et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: No data has established a causal link between pre- and postsynaptic firing to changes in connection strength during behavior prior to this study.
source: While such studies provide strong evidence of plasticity at excitatory-interneuron synapses, so far, no data has established a causal link between pre- and postsynaptic firing to changes in connection strength during behavior.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the literature.

claim: Optogenetic activation of Halorhodopsin or Archaerhodopsin in a subpopulation of pyramidal cells and interneurons led to the inhibition of a subset of pyramidal cells and interneurons.
source: In this study, we optogenetically interfered with the circuit function by activating Halorhodopsin or Archaerhodopsin in a subpopulation of pyramidal cells and interneurons. This manipulation led to the inhibition of a subset of pyramidal cells and interneurons and also light-triggered disinhibition of many pyramidal cells (Gridchyn et al., 2020; Schoenenberger et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citations to prior work.

claim: Optogenetic activation of Halorhodopsin or Archaerhodopsin in a subpopulation of pyramidal cells and interneurons led to light-triggered disinhibition of many pyramidal cells.
source: In this study, we optogenetically interfered with the circuit function by activating Halorhodopsin or Archaerhodopsin in a subpopulation of pyramidal cells and interneurons. This manipulation led to the inhibition of a subset of pyramidal cells and interneurons and also light-triggered disinhibition of many pyramidal cells (Gridchyn et al., 2020; Schoenenberger et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citations to prior work.

claim: Multiple unit and field potential activities were recorded from the dorsal hippocampus in five rats during exploration and quiet immobility sessions.
source: We recorded multiple unit and field potential activities from the dorsal hippocampus in five rats, during exploration and quiet immobility sessions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Halorhodopsin (NpHR-YFP) was expressed in the dorsal CA1 region of the hippocampus in four rats.
source: In these rats, Halorhodopsin (NpHR-YFP, n = 4 rats) or Archaerhodopsin (ArchT, n = 1 rat) was expressed in the dorsal CA1 region of the hippocampus under the control of the CaMKIIα promoter using an adeno-associated virus (AAV2/1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Archaerhodopsin (ArchT) was expressed in the dorsal CA1 region of the hippocampus in one rat.
source: In these rats, Halorhodopsin (NpHR-YFP, n = 4 rats) or Archaerhodopsin (ArchT, n = 1 rat) was expressed in the dorsal CA1 region of the hippocampus under the control of the CaMKIIα promoter using an adeno-associated virus (AAV2/1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Halorhodopsin and Archaerhodopsin were expressed under the control of the CaMKIIα promoter using an adeno-associated virus (AAV2/1).
source: In these rats, Halorhodopsin (NpHR-YFP, n = 4 rats) or Archaerhodopsin (ArchT, n = 1 rat) was expressed in the dorsal CA1 region of the hippocampus under the control of the CaMKIIα promoter using an adeno-associated virus (AAV2/1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: In four rats, fifteen independently-movable tetrodes and one 200 µm optic fiber centered in the middle of the tetrode bundle targeted the dorsal CA1 region.
source: In four rats, fifteen independently-movable tetrodes and one 200 µm optic fiber centered in the middle of the tetrode bundle targeted the dorsal CA1 region while, in the remaining animal, 24 tetrodes and four optic fibers were used (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: In one rat, 24 tetrodes and four optic fibers were used.
source: In four rats, fifteen independently-movable tetrodes and one 200 µm optic fiber centered in the middle of the tetrode bundle targeted the dorsal CA1 region while, in the remaining animal, 24 tetrodes and four optic fibers were used (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Recordings were performed during four 25 min exploration sessions in which first a familiar environment (FAM1) was explored followed by a novel environment (NOV), and finally, the animals were returned to the familiar environment for the remaining two sessions.
source: We recorded during four 25 min exploration sessions in which first a familiar environment (FAM1) was explored followed by a novel environment (NOV), and finally, the animals were returned to the familiar environment for the remaining two sessions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: During the second familiar exploration session laser stimulation was applied (FAML) in a fixed part of the environment but not in the last exploration (FAM2).
source: During the second familiar exploration session laser stimulation was applied (FAML) in a fixed part of the environment but not in the last exploration (FAM2, see Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: In all sessions, neither the average speed nor the occupancy within the light stimulation sector were significantly different, compared to the part of the environment where no light was triggered (all p>0.5607).
source: In all sessions, neither the average speed nor the occupancy within the light stimulation sector were significantly different, compared to the part of the environment where no light was triggered (all p>0.5607).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Monosynaptically-connected pyramidal cell-interneuron pairs were identified by calculating the cross-correlation of their spike firing times and testing for the presence of a short-latency (1–2 ms) sharp (1–2 ms wide) peak.
source: We identified monosynaptically-connected pyramidal cell-interneuron pairs by calculating the cross-correlation of their spike firing times and testing for the presence of a short-latency (1–2 ms) sharp (1–2 ms wide) peak.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The short-latency peak in the cross-correlation indicates the presence of a monosynaptic connection in which the presynaptic pyramidal cell can discharge the postsynaptic interneuron within a short latency.
source: This peak indicates the presence of a monosynaptic connection in which the presynaptic pyramidal cell can discharge the postsynaptic interneuron within a short latency.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about cross-correlation analysis.

claim: The magnitude of the peak in the cross-correlation reflects the connection weight between a given cell pair.
source: In turn, the magnitude of the peak, that is, its transmission probability, reflects the connection weight between a given cell pair.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about cross-correlation analysis.

claim: Changes in firing rate across sessions by either or both cells in the pair would result in an alteration of the magnitude of the peak that does not reflect a change in connection weight, but rather a general change in the probability of joint firing.
source: Changes in firing rate across sessions by either or both cells in the pair would result in an alteration of the magnitude of the peak that does not reflect a change in this connection weight, but rather a general change in the probability of joint firing.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the methodology.

claim: The chance probability that the pair fires together was measured by averaging the correlation probabilities over the 10–50 ms time bins and subtracting this from the peak.
source: To account for this, throughout all the analysis, we measured the chance probability that the pair fires together, by averaging the correlation probabilities over the 10–50 ms time bins and subtracting this from the peak.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: 78 pyramidal cell-interneuron pairs were identified in these recordings.
source: Altogether, we identified 78 pyramidal cell-interneuron pairs in these recordings (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Light application suppressed activity in some cells and triggered an elevated rate through disinhibition in others.
source: The light stimulation inhibited not only a selected population of pyramidal cells but also many interneurons, while a further group of pyramidal cells increased their firing due to disinhibition, as assessed directly by their light responses to brief light pulses in the rest session at the end of the recordings (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Disinhibited pyramidal cells only increased their firing after the maximum light-mediated suppression on interneurons.
source: In our previous work, we showed that these disinhibited pyramidal cells only increased their firing after the maximum light-mediated suppression on interneurons (Gridchyn et al., 2020; Schoenenberger et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Both somatostatin- and parvalbumin immunopositive interneurons can express transgenes following AAV-mediated transduction.
source: We also showed before (Schoenenberger et al., 2016) that both somatostatin- and parvalbumin immunopositive interneurons can express transgenes following AAV-mediated transduction in agreement with earlier work (Nathanson et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Other adeno-associated virus serotypes or the usage of the same virus in other brain regions may yield principal cell-specific expression.
source: It is possible, however, that other adeno-associated virus serotypes or the usage of the same virus in other brain regions may yield principal cell-specific expression.
evidence: The claim is speculative.

claim: Many pyramidal cell - interneuron pairs with monosynaptic connections showed changes in firing rate during the FAML session, when compared to FAM1.
source: As a result, many pyramidal cell - interneuron pairs with monosynaptic connections showed changes in firing rate during the FAML session, when compared to FAM1 (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 1C.

claim: The correlation of the FAM1 vs FAML rates was significantly lower compared to rates measured in alternating 5 s time windows within FAM1, both for pyramidal cells and interneurons (all p<0.0001, Z-test).
source: The altered network activity during the light session is demonstrated by significantly lower correlation of the FAM1 vs FAML rates as compared to rates measured in alternating 5 s time windows within FAM1, both for pyramidal cells and interneurons (all p<0.0001, Z-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: No significant differences were found in the median of FAM1 and FAML firing rates (interneuron p=0.3213 pyramidal cell p=0.1448, Mann-Whitney test).
source: However, no significant differences were found in the median of FAM1 and FAML firing rates (interneuron p=0.3213 pyramidal cell p=0.1448, Mann-Whitney test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The spike transmission probability of pyramidal cell-interneuron pairs was changed during the FAML session.
source: The spike transmission probability of these cell pairs was also changed (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 1D.

claim: The correlation FAM1 vs FAML spike transmission values was lower than that measured in alternating 5 s time windows within FAM1 (p<0.0001, Z-test).
source: As for firing rates, the correlation FAM1 vs FAML spike transmission values was lower than that measured in alternating 5 s time windows within FAM1 (p<0.0001, Z-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: There was a significant reduction in the median of the spike transmission probabilities from FAM1 to FAML (p<0.01. Mann-Whitney test).
source: Moreover, there was a significant reduction in the median of the spike transmission probabilities from FAM1 to FAML (p<0.01. Mann-Whitney test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Light-induced network modifications altered the ability of the pyramidal cell to drive the postsynaptic interneuron, beyond that of the firing rate alterations-mediated changes.
source: Because in the spike transmission measurements the chance probability that cells randomly fire together was compensated for, light-induced network modifications altered the ability of the pyramidal cell to drive the postsynaptic interneuron, beyond that of the firing rate alterations-mediated changes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Changes in connection weight between cell pairs during the FAML session could be either transient or reflect longer-term plasticity that outlasts optogenetic stimulation.
source: Changes in connection weight between cell pairs during the FAML session could be either transient or reflect longer-term plasticity that outlasts optogenetic stimulation.
evidence: The claim is speculative.

claim: Connection strength could change as place cells remap their place fields during exploration of a different environment.
source: Moreover, connection strength could change as place cells remap their place fields during exploration of a different environment (Wilson and McNaughton, 1993).
evidence: The claim is based on citation to prior work.

claim: The absolute value of normalized spike transmission differences between sessions was the largest between NOV-FAM1 and FAML-FAM1 sessions.
source: Overall, this score was the largest between NOV-FAM1 and FAML-FAM1 sessions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Changes between FAM2-FAM1 sessions were about 30% weaker relative to NOV-FAM1 and FAML-FAM1 sessions, but were still significantly larger than zero (all p<0.001; ANOVA).
source: However, while the changes between FAM2-FAM1 sessions were about 30% weaker relative to the others, they were still significantly larger than zero (all p<0.001; ANOVA).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Changes between FAM2-FAM1 sessions were significantly larger than changes within FAM1 sessions as assessed by correlations measured in alternating 5 s time windows (p<0.0268, F-test).
source: In addition, changes between FAM2-FAM1 sessions were significantly larger than changes within FAM1 sessions as assessed by correlations measured in alternating 5 s time windows (p<0.0268, F-test), independent of the variability across animals (p=0. 0562, Likelihood-ratio test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Spike transmissions in FAM2 were strongly predicted by the observed connection weights in all the previous sessions (all p<0.0001, F-test).
source: Spike transmissions in FAM2 were strongly predicted by the observed connection weights in all the previous sessions (all p<0.0001, F-test, Figure 2C), indicating that connection strength between the pairs was only partially reorganized.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 2C.

claim: Connection strength between pyramidal-interneuron pairs was only partially reorganized.
source: Spike transmissions in FAM2 were strongly predicted by the observed connection weights in all the previous sessions (all p<0.0001, F-test, Figure 2C), indicating that connection strength between the pairs was only partially reorganized.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: The variability across animals did not significantly account for variability in the spike transmission in FAM2 (all p>0.5656, Likelihood-ratio test).
source: The variability across animals did not significantly account for variability in the spike transmission (all p>0.5656, Likelihood-ratio test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Both FAM1 and FAML predicted FAM2 spike transmission, independent of the other (all p<0.0105, F-test).
source: We found that both FAM1 and FAML predicted FAM2 spike transmission, independent of the other (all p<0.0105, F-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: NOV no longer predicted FAM2 when the effect of FAM1 was taken into consideration (p=0.4453, F-test).
source: However, the model comparison showed that the NOV no longer predicted FAM2 when the effect of FAM1 was taken into consideration (p=0.4453, F-test) nor the variation across animals contributed (all p>0.5656, Likelihood-ratio test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The changes in connection weights during NOV did not influence the subsequent weights observed in FAM2.
source: Thus, the changes in connection weights during NOV did not influence the subsequent weights observed in FAM2, which instead was explained by weights in both FAM1 and FAML, independently.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Spike transmission values were more similar within the same environmental context.
source: Therefore, while spike transmission values were more similar within the same environmental context, light application significantly biased spike transmission and caused lasting changes in FAM2 relative to FAM1.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Light application significantly biased spike transmission and caused lasting changes in FAM2 relative to FAM1.
source: Therefore, while spike transmission values were more similar within the same environmental context, light application significantly biased spike transmission and caused lasting changes in FAM2 relative to FAM1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Cell pairs in which light application led to a decrease in spike transmission relative to FAM1 also maintained weaker spike transmission values in FAM2 (all p<0.0001, F-test).
source: Indeed, those cell pairs in which light application led to a decrease in spike transmission relative to FAM1 also maintained weaker spike transmission values in FAM2, while cell pairs with light-enhanced transmission showed a persistent increase in transmission probability in FAM2 (all p<0.0001, F-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Cell pairs with light-enhanced transmission showed a persistent increase in transmission probability in FAM2 (all p<0.0001, F-test).
source: Indeed, those cell pairs in which light application led to a decrease in spike transmission relative to FAM1 also maintained weaker spike transmission values in FAM2, while cell pairs with light-enhanced transmission showed a persistent increase in transmission probability in FAM2 (all p<0.0001, F-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The relative change of spike transmission between FAML-FAM1 predicted the score change from FAM1 to FAM2 (p<0.0001, F-test).
source: Moreover, the relative change of spike transmission (difference divided by the sum) between FAML-FAM1 predicted the score change from FAM1 to FAM2 (p<0.0001, F-test), indicating that larger relative changes in spike transmission between FAML-FAM1 were accompanied by similarly larger changes between FAM2-FAM1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Larger relative changes in spike transmission between FAML-FAM1 were accompanied by similarly larger changes between FAM2-FAM1.
source: Moreover, the relative change of spike transmission (difference divided by the sum) between FAML-FAM1 predicted the score change from FAM1 to FAM2 (p<0.0001, F-test), indicating that larger relative changes in spike transmission between FAML-FAM1 were accompanied by similarly larger changes between FAM2-FAM1.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Light-induced changes in neuronal firing during FAML may lead to lasting modifications of spike transmission.
source: Thus, light-induced changes in neuronal firing during FAML may lead to lasting modifications of spike transmission.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Interneuron rate changes of both FAML-FAM1 and FAM2-FAM1 influenced FAM2-FAM1 spike transmission changes, even when each other's influence was taken into account (all p<0.0064, Likelihood-ratio test).
source: We found that interneuron rate changes of both FAML-FAM1 and FAM2-FAM1 influenced FAM2-FAM1 spike transmission changes, even when each other's influence was taken into account (all p<0.0064, Likelihood-ratio test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Pyramidal cell rate changes during FAML no longer significantly influenced FAM2-FAM1 spike transmission changes when FAM2-FAM1 rate change was taken into account (p=0.0999, Likelihood-ratio test).
source: However, pyramidal cell rate changes during FAML no longer significantly influenced FAM2-FAM1 spike transmission changes when FAM2-FAM1 rate change was taken into account (p=0.0999, Likelihood-ratio test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Changes in the excitability of interneurons during the light application influenced the spike transmission strength subsequently in FAM2 even when the FAM2-FAM1 rate alterations of the interneuron were compensated for.
source: This suggests that changes in the excitability of interneurons during the light application, as assessed by rate changes, influenced the spike transmission strength subsequently in FAM2 even when the FAM2-FAM1 rate alterations of the interneuron were compensated for.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: A change in spike transmission in FAM2 did not predict the degree of pyramidal place field remapping (p=0.1612, F-test).
source: In addition to the changing firing rate, the light application can cause remapping in a subpopulation of cells (Schoenenberger et al., 2016). However, a change in spike transmission in FAM2 did not predict the degree of pyramidal place field remapping (p=0.1612, F-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Interneurons that exhibited elevated or reduced firing rate during FAML session exhibited significantly different changes in monosynaptic spike transmission probability across FAM2 and FAM1 (p<0.0001, F-test).
source: Interneurons that exhibited elevated or reduced firing rate during FAML session exhibited significantly different changes in monosynaptic spike transmission probability across FAM2 and FAM1 (p<0.0001, F-test) independent of the variability across animals (p=0.3372, Likelihood-ratio test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Pyramidal cells did not show a relationship between firing rate change during FAML and spike transmission change across FAM2 and FAM1 (p=0.4499, F-test).
source: Pyramidal cells did not show such a relationship (p=0.4499, F-test) and the variability across animals did not influence this result (p=0.1359, Likelihood-ratio test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Suppressed interneurons tended to weaken their monosynaptic weights with presynaptic pyramidal cells.
source: Therefore, suppressed interneurons tended to weaken their monosynaptic weights with presynaptic pyramidal cells, whereas those that increased their rate exhibited increased weights.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Interneurons that increased their rate exhibited increased monosynaptic weights with presynaptic pyramidal cells.
source: Therefore, suppressed interneurons tended to weaken their monosynaptic weights with presynaptic pyramidal cells, whereas those that increased their rate exhibited increased weights.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: The interneuron increase and decrease groups were significantly different in spike transmission changes, independent of the pyramidal increase and decrease as a factor (p<0.0004, F-test).
source: A two-way ANOVA analysis showed that the interneuron increase and decrease groups were significantly different, independent of the pyramidal increase and decrease as a factor (p<0.0004, F-test), but not the pyramidal group (p=0.4067, F-test), and the variability across animals did not influence the result (p=0.2749, Likelihood-ratio test) and no significant interactions were seen between cell pair groups (p=0.6109, F-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The pyramidal group did not show significant differences in spike transmission changes (p=0.4067, F-test).
source: A two-way ANOVA analysis showed that the interneuron increase and decrease groups were significantly different, independent of the pyramidal increase and decrease as a factor (p<0.0004, F-test), but not the pyramidal group (p=0.4067, F-test), and the variability across animals did not influence the result (p=0.2749, Likelihood-ratio test) and no significant interactions were seen between cell pair groups (p=0.6109, F-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The relative change of spike pairing events between FAML and FAM1 predicted significantly FAM2-FAM1 spike transmission change for 50 ms window (p<0.00099, F-test).
source: The relative change (difference/sum) of spike pairing events was calculated between FAML and FAM1 and these spike pairing changes predicted significantly FAM2-FAM1 spike transmission change in all three cases for 50 ms window (p<0.00099, F-test) even when multiple testing correction was performed while the variability across animals did not influence the result (all p>0.3913, Likelihood-ratio test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: In time intervals other than 50 ms, the correlations between spike pairing changes and spike transmission changes were not significant (all p>0.0517, F-test).
source: In the other tested time intervals, the correlations were not significant (all p>0.0517, F-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Spike pairing event number no longer predicted the FAM2-FAM1 spike transmission changes when interneuron and pyramidal changes were together taken into account (all p>0.417, F-test).
source: Moreover, spike pairing event number no longer predicted the FAM2-FAM1 spike transmission changes when interneuron and pyramidal changes were together taken into account, (all p>0.417, F-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Spike pairing itself was strongly predicted (all R2>0.859) by pyramidal and interneuron firing rates.
source: However, spike pairing itself was strongly predicted (all R2>0.859) by pyramidal and interneuron firing rates, explaining why spike transmission changes could not be predicted independently from the combined interneuron and pyramidal rates by spike pairing.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Light-induced, optogenetic alterations of the CA1 network activity can trigger lasting alterations of the monosynaptic spike transmission probability of pyramidal-cell interneuron pairs.
